name: Middle Clarence Bandjalang
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: midd1357 (Middle Clarence Bandjalang) is not in the catalog under this key; the same lect is coded in the catalog as band1339 'Bandjalang' (QS-HEDGED, carried-quote: Hayes 1980 pp.108-109/170 fn.2 and StressTyp2-carried Hammond 1986:193,195, all second-hand on Crowley 1978). The sweep's one item, Hammond 1986 NLLT 4 (DOI 10.1007/BF00133844), is relevant -- the Springer landing page (opened via web lookups) lists Crowley 1978 The Middle Clarence Dialects of Bandjalang in its references and StressTyp2 carries its Bandjalang sentences from pp.193/195 ('Main stress is generally initial, secondary stress on long vowels'; 'Words with main stress on the second vowel are only optional variants') -- but it is paywalled (Springer USD 39.95; Unpaywall closed; S2 closed; not on Hammond's Arizona/GitHub pages; CORE/BASE/IA Scholar blocked), so nothing in it was read first-hand: access = paywalled-doi, priority medium (it is a secondary analysis whose Bandjalang content is already carried verbatim by StressTyp2). The primary that would settle the coding, Crowley 1978 (AIAS, 492 pp; not among the sweep items), remains unreachable: archive.org middleclarencedi0000crow is lending/printdisabled only (metadata re-fetched sources; search-inside 'Item not available'; FTS 0 hits), HathiTrust is search-only and its API returned 403 from our machine, Google Books API quota exhausted, AIATSIS/Austlang behind Cloudflare, ANU Open Research has no Crowley item; priority HIGH for acquisition (library or IA borrow). Best first-hand statement actually read this sweep is Sharpe 1997 (PL C-136) p.372, already on file: stress is initial unless a non-initial syllable has a long vowel ('By Crowley's, the Geytenbeeks' and my analysis, this indicates a long vowel in the syllable perceived as stressed'), corroborating the band1339 coding (initial, long-vowel-sensitive) without superseding it; Wikipedia's Stress section (fetched sources wikitext) attributes the same quantity-sensitive picture to Sharpe 2005:180 (LINCOM grammar, closed). Cunningham 1969:75 (Yugumbir, sister dialect, on file) gives 'first syllable... or the first long syllable if such is present'. All fetch receipts are in with.org/Wikipedia APIs and direct fetches.

new_statements.quote: Watson in particular uses some diacritics on certain vowels. An acute accent indicates stress usually when it falls on other than the first syllable. By Crowley's, the Geytenbeeks' and my analysis, this indicates a long vowel in the syllable perceived as stressed.
new_statements.citation: Sharpe, Margaret C. 1997. Yugambeh-Bundjalung: what can be learnt from the dialect differences. In Darrell Tryon & Michael Walsh (eds), Boundary rider: essays in honour of Geoffrey O'Grady, 363-392. Canberra: Pacific Linguistics C-136.
new_statements.locator: p. 372 (section 1, on transcription conventions; pdf p. 10); cf. p. 368 ('stress-timed') and p. 373 (vowel shortening forced by stress)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: 15144/PL-C136.363, CC BY-SA 4.0 2015 online edition) — extracted text gives the page headed '372 MARGARET C. SHARPE' and the three sentences read exactly as quoted: 'Watson in particular uses some diacritics on certain vowels. An acute accent indicates stress usually when it falls on other than the first syllable. By Crowley's, the Geytenbeeks' and my analysis, this indicates a long vowel in the syllable perceived as stressed.' (text layer lines 447-449; only artefact is scanned spacing 'Crowley' s'). The sentence closes section 1.4 on transcription conventions, immediately before '2. VOWEL SHIFTS RELIABLY NOTED IN THE DIFFERENT DIALECTS'. Corroborating passages in the same paper, verified:…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Default stress is on the first syllable; when stress is heard elsewhere in the word, that syllable is one with a long vowel (vowel length attracts stress). The Waalubal-specific version carried from Crowley 1978 by Hayes 1980:109 / Goedemans 1998 / StressTyp2: main stress on the initial syllable unless the first vowel is short and the second long, in which case on the second; Sharpe 1998:14,16 (Yugambeh, 'as are the other dialects') states it as: the first syllable is stressed except when a long vowel elsewhere in the word takes the primary stress; long vowels are stressed, otherwise the first syllable.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Sharpe 1997 is silent. Second-hand for Waalubal: Hayes 1980:170 fn.2 and Hammond 1986:193 (via StressTyp2) place secondary stress on long vowels; Sharpe 1998:16 adds that two long vowels (almost) never occur in a row, and Sharpe 1997:373 notes vowel shortening forced by the stress pattern.
new_statements.exceptions: 'usually' hedges the initial default. Second-hand: Hammond 1986:195 (via StressTyp2) says words with main stress on the second vowel are only optional variants; StressTyp2/Rice 1992 (Gidabal, pattern 'Exceptional (Waalubal)') reports free variation in L-H disyllables (djuluːn ~ djuˈluːn).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, from wordlist citation forms across the Yugambeh-Bundjalung dialect chain (Sharpe's own Western Bundjalung data plus Crowley's Wahlubal/Wehlubal and the Geytenbeeks' Gidhabal); the sentence is framed as a transcription convention and is indirect, so confidence is medium. The Middle-Clarence-specific primary description (Crowley 1978) was not opened.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog band1339 is the FAMILY node 'Bandjalangic', not a language: the catalog's existing QS-tier unit keyed band1339 'Bandjalang (Waalubal)' (StressTyp2 lect 878, WALS bwa, Crowley 1978) actually describes the Waalubal dialect [waal1238] of Middle Clarence Bandjalang [midd1357], i.e. this language. The quoted Sharpe 1997 statement is chain-wide (Yugambeh-Bundjalung) and explicitly built on Crowley's Wahlubal/Wehlubal (Middle Clarence), the Geytenbeeks' Gidhabal [gida1240] and Sharpe's own Western Bundjalung (Tabulam/Baryulgil = Middle Clarence) data; Sharpe 1998's more direct wording is for Yugambeh [yugu1249, Tweed-Albert]. Cunningham 1969 = Yugumbir [yugu1249]; Livingstone 1892 = Minjangbal [minj1242] (Glottolog files it under midd1357 but it is Tweed-Albert and is silent on stress).

new_statements.citation: Sharpe, Margaret C. 1997. Yugambeh-Bundjalung: what can be learnt from the dialect differences. In D. Tryon & M. Walsh (eds), Pacific Linguistics C-136: 363-392. Canberra: ANU (CC BY-SA; ANU Open Research handle 1885/253898).

new_statements.reading: First-hand statement by a linguist who worked on the whole Yugambeh-Bundjalung dialect chain, explicitly covering Crowley's (Middle Clarence) analysis: the default stressed syllable is the first, and where stress is perceived elsewhere than the first syllable the stressed syllable contains a long vowel -- i.e. initial stress, attracted to a long vowel (CVV-sensitive); it says nothing about which of several long vowels wins or about the disyllabic L-H variation reported by Hayes/Hammond. It is weaker than the (unreached) Crowley 1978 primary and than the StressTyp2-carried Hayes 1980 / Hammond 1986 rule, so it should be read as a corroborating first-hand statement, not as a new deciding source. Consistent with the sister-dialect primaries on file: Cunningham 1969:75 (Yugumbir) 'Stress occurs on the first syllable of the word, or on the first long syllable if such is present', and Hayes 1980:109 (carrying Crowley 1978 for Waalubal) 'the mirror image stress pattern [of Yapese] is reported for... the Waalubal dialect of Bandjalang', fn. 2 p.170 'Banjalang also ha[s] secondary stress, which falls on long vowels'.

sources.note: p.13: 'Like English, Yugambeh is "stress-timed", as are the other dialects of this language.' p.14: 'the first syllable of a word is usually stressed and clear, except when there is a long vowel elsewhere in the word, which then gets the primary stress, and the first syllable is less clear.' p.16: 'Long vowels (all the ones with h written after them) are stressed; otherwise the first syllable of a word is stressed. There are never (or almost never) two long vowels in a row.' Describes Yugambeh (Tweed-Albert), generalised to the chain.
